Low
lō
adj. (not high; humble in station; brought down; rendering Hebrew shaphal, Greek tapeinos)
From the Norse lagr, low. Scripture keeps the physical and the social senses joined to a moral one: the low place is where God characteristically works, and the high place is where He characteristically resists.

Biblical Definition

Low in Scripture is a station rather than a defect, and it is the station God prefers to work from. Mary's song states the principle as a settled divine habit: “He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Luke 1:52). The two clauses are one action; the same providence that lowers the seated mighty raises the low. Job's friend, whatever else he got wrong, states the same rule rightly: God works “To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety” (Job 5:11). The Psalmist writes it into Israel's history as a mercy remembered: “Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psalm 136:23). Low estate is not something the LORD overlooks but something He specifically remembers. James therefore turns the word into a command for rejoicing rather than a cause of shame: “Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted” (James 1:9). The exaltation is present, not merely promised; a poor believer is already raised in Christ, and the Apostle instructs him to reckon it so while his circumstances still say otherwise.

Webster 1828 Definition

Not high or elevated; depressed below the usual level; humble in rank or condition; dejected. Scripture treats low estate as the place God remembers, works from, and exalts, and warns against the high-mindedness that despises it.

expand to see more

LOW, a. [Norm. lagr, low.] Not high or elevated; depressed below any given surface or place; as, low ground; a low situation.

2. Not rising to the usual height; as, a man of low stature.

3. Declining near the horizon; as, the sun is low.

4. Humble in rank or condition; in a state of subjection or inferiority; as, men of low degree.

5. Dejected; depressed in spirits; as, low spirits.

6. Moderate; not high in price; also, not loud; as, a low voice.

Key Scripture

Luke 1:52 — "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree."

Job 5:11 — "To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety."

Psalm 136:23 — "Who remembered us in our low estate: for his mercy endureth for ever:"

James 1:9 — "Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted:"

Modern Corruption

Low estate is treated as a problem to be escaped rather than a place God remembers, and the church has largely adopted the world's scale of seats — platform, influence, and reach — which is exactly the scale the Magnificat says God inverts.

expand to see more

The Magnificat is sung in churches that are organized on the opposite principle. Mary announces a God who puts down the mighty from their seats and exalts them of low degree; the surrounding religious culture measures a ministry by the size of its seat — attendance, platform, reach, influence — and quietly assumes that God is doing His best work wherever the numbers are largest. The two scales cannot both be right. Scripture's consistent testimony is that God chooses the base things and the things that are despised, and that He resists the proud, which means the pursuit of a higher seat is a pursuit of the place where divine resistance is promised.

There is an answering error among the low themselves: to treat low estate as identity and grievance rather than as the place of a present exaltation. James forbids that reading. The brother of low degree is commanded to rejoice, and the ground of the rejoicing is stated in the perfect tense — he is exalted. His circumstances have not changed; his standing has. Recover both halves and the word does its proper work: no man need climb to be remembered, and no man may sulk in the place where God has promised to remember him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaphal (to be low, to be brought low) supplies both the physical and the moral senses; Greek tapeinos (lowly, humble) is the New Testament word for low degree and for the humility God gives grace to.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaphal (H8213) — to be or become low, to be humbled; used of mountains made low and of the proud brought down.

Hebrew dal (H1800) — poor, weak, thin; the low man whom the law protects and the LORD defends.

Greek tapeinos (G5011) — lowly, of low degree, humble; the word of Luke 1:52 and James 1:9.

Greek tapeinoo (G5013) — to make low, to humble; the verb of humbling oneself under the mighty hand of God.

Greek hupsoo (G5312) — to lift up, to exalt; the counterpart action performed upon the low.

Usage

"“Exalted them of low degree” — the raising of the low and the putting down of the mighty are one act."

"“Who remembered us in our low estate” — low estate is remembered, not overlooked."

"“Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted” — the exaltation is present, not merely future."
